<reason>A wins by connecting attachment-based influence to concrete, anticipatory oversight beyond prohibiting individual abusive tactics. Its functional distinction between relationship-centered products and incidentally warm tutors substantially answers B’s scope objection. B raises legitimate compliance-cost concerns, but repeatedly insists that the social analogy requires a crowd rather than answering A’s cumulative-risk mechanism. A more convincingly treats “more like” as a comparison of regulatory duties, not the name of the legal framework housing them.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pressure-question exchange exposed the decisive difference: B expressly rejected pre-launch testing of cumulative emotional pressure. A then clarified that its proposal requires investigating foreseeable design risks, not proving that attachment never occurs. B’s observation that consumer law could host such duties did not establish that its preferred alternative actually supplies them.</best_rebuttal>
